ASRSN:2186380.n: Low terrain aural warning annunciation once during departure climb out. One aural alert after gear retraction, normal climb out prior to acceleration. By the time the alert registered what it was it was over. I continued via the departure without activating maximum thrust. We were approximately 700 feet climbing at V2 via the SID following the flight director.
ASRSN:2186380.s: The pilot reported a single low terrain aural warning during departure climb at 700 feet AGL while following the flight director on the SID. The alert occurred after gear retraction and ended before the pilot could react, so maximum thrust was not activated.

ASRSN:2186389.n: During demonstration of a cross-controlled stall, an idle power, twenty-degree level left bank was initiated at 90 KIAS, followed by input of left rudder to induce a skidding level turn. Rudder input was too abrupt and too large, and the consequent right-bank made in response to maintain level flight induced a similarly abrupt stall without a warning horn. Aircraft rolled left into 135 degrees of bank, followed by an upset recovery.Suggestions: Cross-control rudder input must be gradual and modest to ensure stall warning horn demonstration and immediate recovery, rather than an abrupt stall and departure.
ASRSN:2186389.s: During a cross-controlled stall demonstration at 90 KIAS, the pilot applied abrupt left rudder, causing an unexpected stall without a warning horn and a 135-degree left bank. The pilot recovered from the upset, noting that gradual rudder input is required to ensure proper stall warning and immediate recovery.

ASRSN:2186476.n: Came into shift on Day 0 at XA:00, turn over from swing shift was that the aircraft was down to engine runs for fuel nozzle replacement on the number one engine. Went through paperwork to see what was left and proceeded. Sprayed down ducts in the core section with leak detectant. Aircraft was pushed outside and I proceeded with engine runs. Person A was in the cockpit with me and the other mechanics were downstairs watching the motor and looking it over between runs. Performed all tasks per job card and Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM), no abnormal readings inside the cockpit and the motor even passed the engine idle test and pneumatic engine on test performed through the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD). Mechanics downstairs did not see any leaks either so the engine was closed up and we started finalizing paperwork while the plane was towed to the line. At around XH:00 Day 1 we realized opposite side pressure (OSP) had not been done yet. Person A and I made our way down to the line to run both engines. During runs there was again no abnormal readings and both engines were operating in similar tolerances. The rest of shift proceeded as normal, clocked out at XK:30. At around XW:00 that night I was informed by a coworker that Aircraft X had an engine fire at takeoff around XL:33 that morning and did an in air return to field. Suggestion: I believe high power runs need to be added back into the job card for fuel nozzle changes. This may have been detected with high power runs that were previously removed from the job card. I arrived at work for my Day 0 shift at XA:00. Person B was the acting shift manager, Person C was the shift supervisor, Person D was my Crew Chief (CC), and Person A, Person E and Person F and Person G were my team mates assigned to work Aircraft X for the night. We were initially told by our CC Person D that swing was buttoning up some of the non-routines and overnight maintenance items but the Nozzle change was down to engine runs/operations checks. When we walked to the aircraft, the winglet changed was being buttoned up and swing shift was still working some seats in the interior. While those were happening, I took it upon myself to do a general visual inspection (GVI) of the engine to look for obvious signs of missing parts, loose parts and tight B-nuts. Even though there is a stamp for the installation of each component/part, and even a buyback from a different mechanic to verify the work, it is VERY common for me to find loose bolts, brackets, missing brackets, and even loose or uninstalled B-nuts after getting turn over from swings that the engine is 'completed and ready for runs'. In this particular instance all stamps were previously bought off, and the engine appeared to be complete. At the time I was not familiar with the components that are removed or installed on the RH side of Leap 1B engines for fuel nozzle changes. I did not look at the tube that was not installed correctly because of it hard to see mounting location, and was not aware that it gets removed/installed during its shop visit. Everything appeared normal, so we cleaned up the area and verified paperwork. We had a meeting to discuss who would be doing what role that night. I usually run the engines on the planes, but Person E was in that night and offered to run the engines. I volunteered to drive the TUG and push the plane back to the pad. I drove the tug over and my other team mates hooked up the tow bar and got everything ready. The steering bypass pin was missed and the towbar sheered its pin when we were half way out of the hangar. The manager Person B was next to the plane when this occurred. We immediately stopped, disconnected the towbar and printed the NLG inspection after shearpin. We completed the inspection with no findings. We then went on the hunt to find a tow bar because the one we sheared is the only one at the hangar. We eventually grabbed one from the line, after which we pushed the plane back to the pad without incident. Person F was going to accomplish the runs, Person E was the signalman/ Person A was in the right seat observing, and I was standing on the stairs at the L1 door to verbally notify Person F to cut the fuel when the motor was going to fog for the Leak check. After wet motor shut down, myself and Person E verified there were no fuel leaks. I looked at the left hand side of the motor and Person E looked at the right hand side of the motor. We then closed the engine thrust reversers (TRs) and fan cowls in prep for runs. I stood in the doorway of the cockpit to observe the engine indications during the runs. I observed no abnormal indications at any point. All tests were normal. Myself, Person A and Person E opened the TRs and looked for pneumatic leaks. I inspected the left side and Person E inspected the right side. When we were closing the cowls I briefly looked at Person E's side for obvious signs of leaks. The were no abnormal conditions or signs of leaks or overheating. I was not originally intending on doing the pneumatic checks myself as I am usually running the engines so I did not prep the motor myself for those checks. There was developer on the motor when I verified the leak check after runs, but I am not sure who put it on there. After closing out the nozzle maintenance, we towed the aircraft to the gate. There were still open overnight maintenance items/non-routines that were going to be turned over to days. After moving Aircraft X to the gate, we were told to bring back Aircraft Y to the hangar and startthe overnight maintenance on that plane. A culture of non-accountability exists in ZZZ which allows frequent escapes like this to go unchecked. Often times there are poor turnovers, paperwork errors, parts incorrectly installed or not at all. When things like this happen, it is often caught by other mechanics and corrected without being reported or the offending individual being aware that a mistake was made. Jobcards for the LEAP 1B engine can be confusing at times, and is very inconsistent in how it directs you to do maintenance. Sometimes bouncing you to an Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and back to a figure within the job card. Grave shift is often pushed to extremes to finish these fuel nozzle planes, or other planes after days and swings seems unable to accomplish maintenance within a reasonable time period. Even with Days/Swings working at a slower pace, graves shift consistently receives turnovers of planes that have been signed off up to engine runs, and are not fully assembled. Suggestions: Make job cards clear and concise. If AMTs are making suggestions to have job cards modified to be more clear or improved, those recommendations should be reviewed and adopted in a timely matter. When preparing to end a shift and get ready for turn over, a job should not be stopped halfway through a removal or an installation. Steps need to be completed to a stopping point. for example: if you're going to stab fuel nozzles, they need to be completely torqued and installed before the next shift. If you cannot get all the B nuts connected, or all the mounting bolts final torqued, do not start that process. A culture of accountability needs to be created that ensures when a stamp is missed the stamping individual is made aware of the issue. If a part is not installed correctly or missed the mechanic is made aware. From CC to mechanic and mechanic to mechanic.
ASRSN:2186476.s: Mechanics performed fuel nozzle replacement and engine runs on Aircraft X, but a subsequent engine fire occurred at takeoff. The reporter attributes the incident to a missing tube installation and suggests that removing high-power runs from the job card prevented detection of the fault.

ASRSN:2186501.n: I was coming from ZZZ1 to ZZZ I was on long right base for Runway XX when I realized a loss of power, I started the re start up actions in my cockpit but I realized that the engine wasn't running, I immediately contacted with the Tower and let them know I was having a problem with my engine, They asked me if it was for fuel, I said I don't know, maybe, but when I took off from ZZZ1 I was with more than 13 gallons which accomplished with the VFR minimums, destination+30 minutes, the flight is 1:10h and my aircraft burns about 5.6gph, I had to land in a field and anyone got hurt and the aircraft didn't suffer any structural damage.
ASRSN:2186501.s: The pilot experienced an engine power loss on long right base for Runway XX while flying from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. Despite having sufficient fuel, the engine failed to restart, forcing a field landing with no injuries or structural damage to the aircraft.

ASRSN:2186510.n: We landed on runway 1L at LAS at XA13. We were following an air carrier on final and Airrcraft Y behind us. We were given 170 KTS till '4-5 mile final' from approach which we complied with, to the 4 mile final.We followed the glide slope on the ILS to touch down zone. (In visual conditions). Over the numbers, we experienced a slight tailwind and light turbulence that caused a longer landing roll out.Abeam N taxi way, we were asked to vacate N. We were still slowing and at this point we were already passing N and we were not at a safe taxi speed for the 90 degree turn. Then the tower asked us to vacate high speed M taxiway to the right. We came to a safe taxi speed for the right turn (slightly passed the leading lines for high speed exit) but before we could commence the 90 degree right turn, we were instructed to make a left turn on J which we did. Aircraft Y behind us was asked to go around between the instructions to vacate N and then later to vacate M. (at least that is to the best of my recollection).While still vacating the runway, we were advised of our possible deviation. We asked tower to standby as we were busy going thru our flow and figuring out where the FBO wanted us to go. Once parked on the ramp and passengers were gone, I attempted to contact the tower at XA28 but no one picked up and went to some answering device. I then called back at XA29 and a controller answered the phone.I inquired as to what the issue was. I had to ask 3-4 times before the controller finally told me that we should have vacated on taxiway M, which we were trying to do.From what I gather, the issue was the go around with Aircraft Y. I am not sure what the spacing looked like but we had to slow to a safe taxi speed to be able to vacate the runway either to the left or the right. It would have been helpful if tower would have communicated their expectation and/or request for vacating the runway before we actually land so we could have briefed it in advance and made every effort to safely accommodate their request.Also important to note that while on final, tower asked Aircraft Y (assuming the one behind us) if they could accept runway 1R which they did not. Based on that, I would assume that there were concerns with the spacing in advance of us landing. Again we did everything we could to help but we did not deviate from anything. Safety first and there was no way we could have taken taxiway N.
ASRSN:2186510.s: The pilot reported that while landing at LAS, conflicting tower instructions to vacate taxiways N, M, and J caused a potential deviation due to the need to slow for safe turns. The pilot attributed the confusion to spacing issues with a trailing aircraft that went around and criticized the lack of pre-landing exit expectations.

ASRSN:2186514.n: During an Instructional Flight for an aircraft checkout a ruff running engine was encountered. On runup the left mag was fouled but was cleaned out by leaning the mixture. On takeoff to 1500 msl feet the engine ran very smoothly. Five minutes into the flight at 1500 msl flying up to 2500 msl the engine started to fun ruff and vibrate. We changed the rpm's from 2500 to 2300 to 2200 and back to 2500 with the engine still vibrating and running ruff. The student asked ZZZ approach to return to airport for landing. When asked if there was a problem the student said that the engine was running ruff but no need to [request assistance] and he want to land as precaution. When returning to the airport we performed the checklist for engine loss and put the carb heat on, gas to fullest tank, fuel pump on, mixture rich, primer in and locked, megs on both, etc. Engine continued to run ruff. On final we put the prop full forward and brought the power back to idle. The engine started to cough so we increase the power slightly. We landed without incident and taxied back to parking. When taxing to parking the engine continued to run slightly ruff.
ASRSN:2186514.s: During an instructional checkout flight, a student pilot and instructor experienced a rough-running engine at 2,500 feet MSL that persisted despite RPM changes and checklist procedures. The crew returned to the airport as a precaution, landing safely while the engine continued to run slightly rough during taxi.

ASRSN:2186519.n: My student and I were underneath class bravo shelf. He was climbing a bit too close to the shelf at 6000 MSL so I told him he needed to descend. He was probably would have gone into it if I didn't say anything. However, the densely populated area was only roughly 4700 MSL. So it was a very tight margin for us to work with to remain high enough over the densely populated area but below the bravo shelf. Anyway, he descended a bit too much and we were less than 1000AGL. We were lined up with the runway on final, but still pretty far out. I think that the airspace is just really tight in that area and it's hard for students in general. I feel like it would help if the bravo shelf was raised even 100 ft higher.
ASRSN:2186519.s: An instructor and student flying a training aircraft on final approach descended below 1,000 feet AGL while maneuvering between a densely populated area at 4,700 MSL and a Class Bravo shelf at 6,000 MSL. The instructor attributed the tight vertical margin to restrictive airspace, suggesting the shelf be raised to improve safety for student pilots.

ASRSN:2186520.n: My crew and I, were conducting regularly scheduled passenger flight operations from ZZZ airport to ZZZ1 airport. We had conducted and completed all taxi phase checklists and made the appropriate radio call stating our intentions to depart the uncontrolled field from Runway XX with an expected right downwind departure to the southeast. We then conducted our 'Take off checklist' without beginning any movement or crossing the hold short boundary into the runway environment, this took us approximately 30 seconds. We both listened and searched both approach ends for traffic. At no point between start up, turning our avionics on, taxi, and crossing the hold short boundary did we hear any radio call on the local CTAF for the area, discerning any inbound or outbound traffic. Almost immediately after our nose crossed the hold short boundary, my copilot and I saw, heard, and acknowledged traffic flying towards us approximately 25' above from the direction of Runway XY. After the incident we queried the pilot of the conflict aircraft and asked if he made a radio call, he said he did however just a 6 mile inbound call. After the incident, both my copilot and wondered how we could have missed him both verbally or visually, it was concluded the pilot of the conflict aircraft did not make anymore position reports and when we entered the runway environment his aircraft must have been in our high wing blind spot.
ASRSN:2186520.s: The flight crew of a passenger aircraft experienced a runway incursion at an uncontrolled airport while entering Runway XX. The conflict occurred because the other pilot failed to make position reports, placing his aircraft in the crew's high-wing blind spot despite a prior 6-mile inbound call.

ASRSN:2186522.n: Intermittent illumination of the 'Alternator INOP' light at 6000 in IMC, direct ZZZZZ intersection to join the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ1 airport. This light was monitored for the majority of the return flight, presumed to be an error with the light, since the other avionics seemed to indicate the battery was still charging. 30mi from ZZZ [airport], an error presented itself on the G5 PFD (Primary Flight Display) which indicated it had lost communication with an air data computer (ADC) or some portion of one. Since we were already aware of the potential for an alternator issue we prompted ATC for a descent out of IMC and to amend our plan to an approach at ZZZ then to ZZZ2 [airport]. The PFD error was followed by an alert on the GPS that ADSB in and out had been lost. We were informed by ZZZ APP that we were no longer on their radar scope, not even a primary target. This was followed by other associated errors, and the battery dying which left only the PFD and HSI on their independent batteries. Communication was retained with ZZZ approach via phone and hand-held radio. We landed without incident at ZZZ.Prior to this incident, a new engine had been installed in the aircraft. The aircraft had approximately 13 hours since this installation of flight time.
ASRSN:2186522.s: The pilot reported intermittent alternator and avionics failures in IMC shortly after a new engine installation, causing total radar loss and battery depletion. The crew descended to VMC, amended their plan, and landed safely at ZZZ using independent battery power and handheld radios.

ASRSN:2186534.n: Climbing through FL300 we hit wake turbulence. Autopilot was on. Seatbelt sign was on. Aircraft quickly rolled 12 degrees to the right. Autopilot stayed on during the event and corrected. I was informed of 2 FAs who received minor injuries during the event when I went back for the second break.
ASRSN:2186534.s: During climb through FL300 with autopilot engaged, the aircraft encountered wake turbulence and rolled 12 degrees right before the autopilot corrected. Two flight attendants sustained minor injuries during the event.

ASRSN:2186543.n: We encountered mountain wave while flying in cruise flight level at FL400 with airspeed deviations of +/- 20 knots and 240+/200- altitude. We notified ATC of the deviations and requested FL380. We were approved and descended to FL380 and the conditions improved. We then heard several aircraft report to ATC they were also encountering similar mountain wave conditions. We notified Dispatch of the encounter at FL400 and the improved conditions at FL380.
ASRSN:2186543.s: The crew encountered mountain wave turbulence at FL400, causing airspeed and altitude deviations. After ATC approved a descent to FL380, conditions improved, and the crew reported the encounter to Dispatch.

ASRSN:2186627.n: After landing, clearance to cross Rwy 26L and taxi behind an airliner south on JJ and to hold short of P advise if the gate is open. Approaching Y1 while southbound on JJ, we advised ATC that the gate was open. A clearance was then given to turn left on Y2 and proceed to the Ramp Spot A. It was very dark and I was having a problem trying to identify where Y2 was. I never saw the painted" Y2 on the ground/taxiway and passed it. We passed Y2 and stopped short of P, while Aircraft X was on taxiway P. Aircraft X was very hard to see but he stopped as too when he saw us approaching Taxiway P. ATC asked if we could make the turn back to Y2 and we advised we were unable. Then ATC advised Aircraft X to continue on P if he had clearance. They did have plenty of clearance and continued as cleared on taxiway P. A new clearance was issued to us to turn left behind Aircraft X then left on taxiway W and to spot A. Cause: The area of JJ near Y1 and Y2 is very dark and does not have taxiway lights or taxiway signage with lights. I was trying to find the signage for Y2 but never saw it. The use of the AMM (Airport Moving Map) on my EFB was not helpful as it was lagging and did not show our actual current position. Suggestions: The area around JJ/Y1/Y2 is very difficult to navigate at night with very little lighting on the and defining the taxiways. The area should be listed as a hotspot with the threats of the area listed for it." On Taxi in we had a near collision event. After landing on RW30 in MIA we cleared at Taxiway Z. Tower instructed us to turn right on Taxiway P and contact ground on frequency. We checked in with ground and were instructed to taxi P to the gate. The FO then went to radio 2 to contact ramp control. As we approached Taxiway JJ I noticed an airliner approaching taxiway P in front of us. I stopped the aircraft and asked ground about the aircraft. He said, Oh yeah, give way to that aircraft. So, I waited for the aircraft to pass and then slowly proceeded into the intersection of P and JJ. As I moved forward I noticed Aircraft Y rapidly approaching us form the left on taxiway JJ. I immediately stopped and pulled to the left and said to ground, what about Aircraft Y here. At that point Aircraft Y braked hard to stop before hitting us. Ground control said, Aircraft Y you missed your turn at Y2. At that point Ground control cleared us to continue the taxi which we were able to do by moving farther to the right to get around Aircraft Y. Then we proceeded to the ramp without further incident. Not sure what the pilots of Aircraft Y were doing but we think they would have hit us if I didn't say something or stop and maneuver our aircraft.Cause: Ground Control in Miami has become a nightmare at certain times of the day. Controllers are making mistakes as are some pilots with taxi instructions and readbacks. This has to improve or there will probably be an accident in the future.
ASRSN:2186627.s: Two separate taxiway incidents occurred at MIA involving a pilot and Aircraft X or Y due to poor lighting, missing signage, and controller errors. The first involved missing a turn on Y2 in the dark, while the second resulted in a near collision when Aircraft Y missed its turn and approached the reporting aircraft on Taxiway JJ.

ASRSN:2186646.n: On approach to Runway XXL, descending into clouds around 6000' with reported rime icing, we began to encounter airspeed related anomalies. Specifically, as we configured with flaps, the max maneuver/min maneuver speed bands converged with corresponding max/stall speed bars also converging on both Primary Flight Displays (PFDs). No 'IAS DISAGREE' msg, however I was unable to engage VNAV when cleared and as the bands converged it became apparent that we had a problem. I disconnected autopilot and around 2600' initiated a soft go around. As I was concerned with our stall margin, I did not change configuration until I was safely in climb with speed increasing. Our airspeeds were in sync with each other and the groundspeed so at that point I then performed full go around maneuver. We [requested priority handling] and once above the clouds I directed FO to the airspeed unreliable checklist. I suspected that icing was the culprit and as the FO ran the checklist we concurred that our airspeeds were accurate and it was likely an indication problem with our speed warning systems due to the icing. Both of our alternates had been reported as overcast (OVC), so we decided to reattempt an approach to ZZZ and requested vectors again for the ILS XXL. This time, I disengaged both the autothrottle/autopilot for the approach and asked the FO to monitor all airspeeds and call out anything less than 160kts(vref was 148). I flew the approach maintaining a higher than normal speed to stay above the min maneuver band. Since the Airspeed (AS) unreliable checklist didn't exactly reflect our situation, I decided that during the approach any stall warning indications would be respected. At some point during the approach we got the 'Leading Edge (LE) FLAPS TRANSIT' light on. As far as I know, we never exceeded any flap speeds or aircraft limits during the event. We landed, left the flaps down and had Airport Rescue and Firefighting inspect the aircraft, particularly our flight controls because we still had transit light. Everything appeared normal and we proceeded to our gate. Postflight inspection revealed some rime ice on the Leading Edge Devices (LEDs) and Maintenance discovered icing in the slat tracks. Cause: Icing. We had covered it in our brief and selected engine anti-ice but I never considered turning on the wing anti-ice and in retrospect realize that it may have mitigated some of our issues. Wing anti-ice is used so rarely that I tend to focus on the restrictions/limitations over the reasons to use it. Not anymore! Time. After [requesting priority handling] I felt time constrained because in the back of my mind I was concerned about our plan B. I knew the ceiling/vis should not be a problem getting into ZZZ, but was not sure how far we might need to go if we couldn't safely get below the OVC layer and needed an alternate with no ice on the arrival. In the rush to get back into the approach I did not give the Flight Attendants (FAs) a precautionary landing brief. I also opted to continue the approach with the transit light on because we knew it was icing related and that would take several minutes of checklist. Checklist. The airspeed unreliable checklist was our initial response to the indications, however the checklist does not consider an event that presents initially as unreliable airspeed but then once checklist is completed we still encounter PFD speed warnings anomalies. I would recommend a decision tree that considers if all airspeed indications are accurate, that icing accumulation may be a factor and direct accordingly with winganti-ice and speed additives for approach.
ASRSN:2186646.s: The flight crew encountered airspeed warning anomalies and a flap transit light during an ILS approach due to rime icing in slat tracks, caused by failing to activate wing anti-ice. They executed a go-around, reattempted the approach manually with higher speeds, and landed safely after a post-flight inspection confirmed the icing.

ASRSN:2186708.n: Master warning light flashed as well as a light on the MWP (Master Warning Panel). Too quick to read so we scanned and found the battery temperature gauge in the red. We [requested priority handling] and Initiated a diversion to ZZZ airport while running the appropriate checklists. Landed without incident. Master warning annunciation went off and a light on the master warning panel illuminated. But we could not read it before it went away. After this the Captain noticed the battery temp gauge was in the red and we started working on the applicable checklists and [requested priority handling]. Chose ZZZ airport as an alternate as we thought it would be the quickest way to get on the ground. Arrived on the ground with no issue.Suggestions: MX (Maintenance) issues nothing to really prevent.
ASRSN:2186708.s: The crew experienced a master warning and red battery temperature gauge indication during flight, prompting a priority diversion to ZZZ airport. They executed checklists and landed without incident, attributing the event to a maintenance issue with no preventable cause.

ASRSN:2186717.n: We were the first flight going into ZZZ with a storm in the area. The winds were gusting up to 47 knots with ATC getting weather updates real time that were a bit delayed in sharing that information with us. We had to divert to ZZZ1.Cause: There was a runway change due to a bad storm right over the field of ZZZ. We were setup for the ILS XX into ZZZ but they switched runways to do the ILS XY. Weather was being updated in real time so ATC could only give us the weather they had which was the ceilings being indefinite and the visibility at 2.5 miles. Winds were also reported at a gust of 47 knots slightly off the right. During the approach, we got a terrain warning when I disconnected the autopilot. I had a stable rate of descent and I could see the runway visually but shortly after, we got the red windshear alert. We did the escape maneuver that quickly went away so we configured for the normal go around profile. In the climb we were about 200 lbs over our bingo fuel so we diverted to the ZZZ1.Suggestion: Hold prior to the approach until weather is updated. A storm was moving from west to east. We were the first aircraft to arrive in ZZZ with the storm moving in. ATC didn't update ATIS although there were significant changes, including wind shifts and significant increases in velocity, resulting in a runway change from Runway XX to XY. Winds after finding out the runway change was 240 @ 20 gusting 47 at the peak. We were setup on the ILS XY, around 700 ft AGL GPWS terrain occurred. Shortly after around 400 ft AGL we received a red wind shear warning. Captain did the escape maneuver and made the decision to divert due to weather. We evaluated fuel and the weather and decided that was the safest course of action. We diverted to ZZZ1 and got in with no issue.Suggestion: Hold to attempt to wait out weather.
ASRSN:2186717.s: The crew of the first flight into ZZZ encountered a storm causing a runway change from ILS XX to XY, triggering terrain and windshear warnings during the approach. After executing an escape maneuver and go-around, they diverted to ZZZ1 due to low fuel and deteriorating weather conditions.

ASRSN:2186833.n: While in cruise at FL380, we received at R Eng Ovht caution message. It was preceded momentarily by an N1 reduction on the same side. Per the QRH, the message extinguished once the thrust lever was reduced to idle. At this time we were roughly 230 miles from ZZZ1 airport and 250 from ZZZ airport. The CA conferred with Dispatch and we made the decision to divert to ZZZ. Once the decision was made, the flight went uneventfully and we landed safely in ZZZ and taxied to the gate. We debriefed with ourselves, Maintenance, and the Chief Pilot upon arrival.
ASRSN:2186833.s: The flight crew experienced an R Eng Ovht caution and N1 reduction at FL380, which cleared after reducing thrust to idle. They diverted to ZZZ airport, landing safely and debriefing with maintenance and the Chief Pilot.

ASRSN:2186847.n: I was pilot flying at the time. Event started around 11,000 ft when ATC instruction was given for descent, lateral navigation for approach and altimeter setting given. ATC specifically gave us 29.72 for altimeter setting and intercept altitude for GPS approach XX (at or above 3500 at ZZZZZ). Crew member read back instruction and no correction was made by ATC. This lead us to believe that was the correct actions/settings. I believe just outside of ZZZZZ is where event was identified by ATC. He told us we were somewhere around 3100 ft instead of our presumed 3500 ft that we saw on our altimeters. Terrain function was on during the descent and approach and terrain was briefed prior. No terrain warning/indications were heard/seen in cockpit. However as soon as ATC mentioned that we were lower, immediate climb was executed. Actions that could have been taken on my end was to verify/question altimeter setting again with ATC even though no correction was given. Upon descent and handed off to approach, I checked in with approach at 11,000' and gave them my altitude and the weather information. The approach controller gave me the altimeter setting 29.72'. Moments later he cleared us to 3,500'. When we got to 3500' he told us to climb immediately. I asked him what the altimeter setting was and I think he told us 29.30'…my captain and I reviewed the tapes online and found him to be incorrect. It seems the altimeter setting may have actually been 29.27', not 29.72'. We did not receive a terrain alert. Backing up, this occurred when we were cleared direct to ZZZZZ on the RNAV XX approach. The MSA is 3700', and the crossing altitude at ZZZZZ is 3100'. The controller told us he showed our aircraft at 3100'. We were given an incorrect altimeter setting. This led to a possible deviation. The surrounding weather patterns were shifting and when they told us 29.72' it didn't seem out of the ordinary. I personally think the controller had a dyslexic moment, and meant to tell us 29.27'. Actions on my end could've been to verify the altimeter setting.
ASRSN:2186847.s: The pilot flying received an incorrect altimeter setting of 29.72 from ATC during descent for an RNAV approach, causing the aircraft to descend to 3100 ft instead of the cleared 3500 ft. ATC identified the deviation and ordered an immediate climb, attributing the error to the controller likely misstating the setting as 29.72 instead of 29.27.

ASRSN:2186848.n: Departing Runway XX at ZZZ climbing to 3000 ft the Pilot Flying observed the pitch limit indicator and the low speed awareness tape increasing due to MAN SPEED selected. The Pilot Flying observed the pitch limit indicator and the low speed awareness tape increasing. Cause: During the Before Takeoff Checklist MAN SPEED selection was not checked deselected by the Pilot Flying during the TOGA/FLIGHT GUIDANCE PANEL check. The Pilot Flying disengaged the auto throttles, advanced the throttles, reduced the aircraft pitch and asked for MAN SPEED deselection. A stick shake was felt during recovery. Suggestions: Confirm MAN SPEED is deselected before takeoff per the checklist
ASRSN:2186848.s: The Pilot Flying departed Runway XX at ZZZ climbing to 3000 ft with MAN SPEED selected, causing pitch limit and low speed awareness tape increases. The pilot recovered by disengaging auto throttles and reducing pitch after a stick shake, attributing the event to failing to deselect MAN SPEED during the before takeoff checklist.

ASRSN:2186894.n: Departure from ZZZ, field elevation 5673'. Tower closed, non-controlled take off runway XXR, no moon. Field MSA 14,800'. First fix on filed flight plan: ZZZZZ, 235 degrees for 85nm. Clearance from ZZZ Approach was 'cleared as filed ZZZ1, climb to FL230…', no SID assigned. We therefore briefed and planned textual ODP: initial takeoff heading 350 to 113 deg. Then, regardless of initial on course heading, turn right 142 degrees, intercept 280 radial to ZZZ2 VOR and climb in holding till above 16,500', then on course. Waypoint for ZZZ2 VOR was loaded to facilitate the textual ODP (Obstacle Departure Procedure).Release instructions from ZZZ approach were to climb heading 350. Takeoff performed, flaps raised at 1500' AGL (roughly 7100' MSL) when ZZZ approach directed: 'left turn direct ZZZZZ.' Left turn commenced with trepidation, which immediately resulted in a solid RED display on GPWS, solid red GPWS display across entire PFD (Primary Flight Display) …inside of 25 nm ring. We were still just climbing thru 10,000' MSL. So, without asking permission, we exercised urgent authority, clicked off auto-pilot and immediately commenced a climbing right turn to avoid impending terrain impact. ZZZ2 was then notified of our deviation from their vectors. Flight to destination completed without any further incidents. ZZZ approach ATC tried to vector us into mountains below MVA, 6000' below MSA.Suggestions ZZZ approach ATC issue to correct.
ASRSN:2186894.s: Pilots departing ZZZ on a non-controlled takeoff received vectors from Approach that directed them toward terrain below the Minimum Safe Altitude. The crew executed an urgent unauthorized climbing right turn to avoid a GPWS terrain warning after ATC issued a left turn that would have caused a mountain impact.

ASRSN:2186895.n: On approach to ILS 06 the FO armed the approach at approximately 20 NM. The aircraft pick up a false localizer and wanted to turn to the right which was not in line with the actual approach. The FO cancelled the APPR mode. NAV mode was used for another 5NM. The ILS APPR was rearmed. GS* and LOC* appeared. GS was active and the LOC did not capture. The ND (Navigation Display) showed the course was off to the right. I asked the FO to come right to where the LOC was. I asked tower if they were any alarms for the LOC. They stated there were none. I was about to call for the G/A (Go Around) when the FO stated he did not have it and said that I have the controls. It was at this time the GPWS CAUTION posted. I immediately performed the Memory Items for EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) Caution at night. The aircraft was cleaned up and we were vectored back to the now requested RNAV 06 approach. I transferred the controls back to the FO. The approach and landing proceeded without incident. After landing the tower stated they completely reset the ILS 06. Another flight was doing the ILS 06 approach. The tower asked them if the LOC was readable. They stated that it appeared to be shifting but was now reading correctly. Tower stated it may have been a power spike. Monitor the approach more closely and call for GA sooner.
ASRSN:2186895.s: The crew experienced a false localizer capture and EGPWS caution during the ILS 06 approach due to a suspected ground power spike. They executed a go-around, switched to an RNAV 06 approach, and landed safely after the tower reset the ILS.

ASRSN:2186908.n: During the crew swap at ZZZ, the Captain of the inbound flight from ZZZ1, Flight Number XXXX, reported that during the approach to ZZZ the aircraft sustained a bird strike on the lower right side of the aircraft below the root of the right wing. Maintenance and Dispatch were notified of the bird strike and during the subsequent maintenance inspection of the aircraft ZZZ Maintenance personnel discovered that the Number One engine had also experienced a bird strike. Consequently, the passengers and flight crew deplaned and the aircraft was taken by ZZZ Maintenance to complete required inspections on the Number One engine.Suggestion: Continue to remain vigilant for wildlife activity and promptly report any suspected encounters with wildlife to ensure required inspections are completed. Good job on the part of ZZZ Maintenance personnel in discovering the additional bird strike on the Number One engine which, if not discovered, could have resulted in further damage to the engine and possible engine failure in flight.
ASRSN:2186908.s: The Captain of Flight XXXX reported a bird strike on the right wing during approach to ZZZ. Maintenance subsequently discovered an additional strike on Engine One, leading to deplaning and required inspections to prevent potential engine failure.

ASRSN:2186949.n: During CLB (Climb) we noticed RIGHT MLG failed to retract. Both RED/GREEN indications on RT gear only. All other gear indications normal.FM (Flight Manual) QRH procedures referenced. Dispatch and Maintenance Control notified. We elected to air return ZZZ. [Priority handling was requested]. Overweight Landing FM procedure referenced. Uneventful air return to ZZZ performed. Two ELB (Electronic Logbook) reports made for MLG and OVERWEIGHT LANDING. Approximate ACGW (Aircraft Gross Weight) at landing was 181.7. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) vehicles followed aircraft to gate.
ASRSN:2186949.s: During climb, the crew observed the right main landing gear failed to retract with only red/green indications, prompting a return to ZZZ. The aircraft landed overweight at 181.7 ACGW following QRH procedures, with ARFF vehicles escorting it to the gate.

ASRSN:2186951.n: After calling rotate on a max power bleeds off, flaps 25 takeoff from ZZZZ, my Primary Flight Display (PFD) airspeed jumped around 30 knots as the FO rotated. The airspeed rapidly fell back slightly below rotate a second later. There were no cells within 15 miles, and the winds were 070 6 [knots] Gusting 17. Acceleration on all airspeed indicators was normal. I did not see the speed on standby or FO PFD during the short event. ZZZZ has unusual winds, but the aircraft did not react as if hit by a massive 30 degree off gust. The FO did not notice the speed on his PFD as he was rotating toward the end of the runway. He did not feel any massive gust during the rotation. All airspeed indications, ground speed, control and performance indications were normal after liftoff. The rest of the flight was uneventful. There had been heavy rain on the ground while parked.
ASRSN:2186951.s: During a takeoff from ZZZZ in heavy rain, the Captain's PFD airspeed briefly jumped 30 knots then dropped as the First Officer rotated. The crew observed no gusts or aircraft reaction, and all indications returned to normal after liftoff with an uneventful flight.

ASRSN:2186980.n: We turned down the aircraft due to an 'Engine Control Mode(s) Inoperative. It included inop A/THR (Auto Throttle), CAT 3, ALPHA FLOOR and BETA TARGET. Procedural it required Flight Directors off on both takeoff and missed approach - two critical phases of flight. I was conducting IOE leg #3 for new hire First Officer. When I called Dispatch, she said the aircraft had been turned down by another crew and that Maintenance was aware that I was conducting training when they assigned the aircraft to me for both an ZZZ-ZZZ1 and ZZZ1-ZZZ2 legs and approximately 8 hours of flying. There were low ceilings and windshear advisories in effect in ZZZ and low ceilings in ZZZ2. Not the best decision in my judgement.
ASRSN:2186980.s: The Captain conducting IOE training for a new First Officer turned down an aircraft due to inoperative engine control modes, including A/THR and CAT 3. Dispatch assigned the aircraft despite known maintenance issues and adverse weather, which the Captain judged as a poor decision.

ASRSN:2186981.n: Received the final weights normally and they were as expected. Received the performance datalink uplink but those numbers were off by about 40,000 lbs. it appeared that the actual takeoff gross weight had gotten put in the zero fuel weight box which then pushed the gross takeoff weight much higher than it should have been. We messaged dispatch and asked for a new uplink. Also talked to the station who then called load planning. The next uplink had the same error. The actual final numbers were confirmed and matched what the flight plan was based on. We ended up manually entering the numbers into the FMS. Flight proceeded as normal.We messaged dispatch.
ASRSN:2186981.s: The flight crew received incorrect performance datalink uplinks where takeoff gross weight was erroneously entered as zero fuel weight, inflating the calculated weight by 40,000 lbs. After dispatch and load planning failed to correct the error, the crew manually entered the verified weights into the FMS, and the flight proceeded normally.

ASRSN:2186983.n: Arrived at the airplane at Gate XX, ZZZ-ZZZ1. While doing our preflight flows and checks the First Officer (FO) said the TCAS would not test and we both had TCAS Fail Flags. I tried to test the TCAS and the same result occurred. In my preflight prep I had noticed that the TCAS system had been written up previously. I wrote it up in the ELB and we called Maintenance. Maintenance came out and they said they could not get the system to test at all. I told them it had been previously written up and they said yes it's got history on it. They asked me what I wanted done and I said let's fix it. They had to check if they had a part. A few mins passed and then on their radios I heard just MEL it. The line maintenance employee, that was in the flight deck responded on the radio, well the Captain wants it fixed. Maintenance then stated well we don't care what the Captain wants. Then the volume was turned down on their radios. With the chronic write ups (which was stated in the MEL write up in the ELB) and our leg was to ZZZ1 (high occurrence of TCAS events in any weather), and I've had multiple RA's and TA's, I made the decision to not operate this aircraft. I then I contracted Dispatch and talked with Maintenance Control and followed that with a conversation with the chief pilot.Another Aircraft was found (#xxxx) we did our preflight checks, boarded up and flew to ZZZ1. Side note on this leg (at Altitude) we got a TA from an aircraft descending.
ASRSN:2186983.s: The Captain and First Officer found a TCAS failure on a preflight check at Gate XX, which maintenance refused to fix despite the Captain's request. The crew cancelled the flight, swapped to another aircraft, and later received a Traffic Advisory while en route to ZZZ1.

ASRSN:2187045.n: We were cleared to taxi to runway 18L. We began our taxi across Zulu (Z) on Hotel Yankee (HY) and began to make the turn onto Yankee (Y) to join Hotel (H). The First Officer noticed Aircraft Y taxiing east on taxiway Yankee (Y) and simultaneously Ground asked us to hold our position and stated 'sorry about that'. We came to a stop without incident. Aircraft Y hit his brakes and the aircraft appeared to put heavy pressure on his nose wheel and then the counter reaction appeared to strike his tail on the taxiway. Ground asked if he was able to 'get around him', there was no response. We were then cleared 'after Aircraft Y you can continue, thanks for your help'. After this the flight was completed without incident.Cause: Aircraft Y was cleared to cross runway 18L and contact east ground on Yankee (Y) bridge. We were cleared from our spot to runway 18L via across and full length. Both clearances allowed aircraft to cross paths. Suggestions: I believe one issue is aircraft being on different frequencies. Clearance to Aircraft Y across runway and then east side ground frequency while being on congested taxiways on west side. Upon approaching the intersection of taxiway HY and taxiway Y we noticed a fast moving Aircraft Y from the left. The Captain quickly, but smoothly brought the aircraft to a complete stop. Aircraft Y noticed us a little bit later and came to a very abrupt stop, striking its tail on the concrete. We didn't hear Aircraft Y so we assumed they were on a different frequency at the time. Due to the angle of the taxi way, and the placement of the cockpit pillars, we did not spot the aircraft crossing sooner.
ASRSN:2187045.s: The crew and Aircraft Y experienced a taxiway conflict at the intersection of taxiways HY and Y due to conflicting clearances and different ground frequencies. Aircraft Y struck its tail on the concrete during an abrupt stop, while the reporting crew stopped safely without incident.

ASRSN:2187069.n: On final approach we experienced what I believed to be wake turbulence. We could see the preceding aircraft ahead and we were closing on them. We elected to slow for the safety of passengers, crew, and aircraft.Cause: Long night flight and tight proximity to aircraft ahead and behind. From what I can remember I believe we had slowed because we encountered some type of turbulence that we believed to be wake turbulence and at some point on final approach we believed we were close to aircraft in front of us within the final approach segment any slowing down was necessary to ensure the safety of the flight.Cause: End of long night landing in LHR.
ASRSN:2187069.s: The pilot reported experiencing suspected wake turbulence on final approach to LHR while closing on a preceding aircraft. The crew elected to slow down to ensure safety due to the long night flight and tight proximity to other traffic.

ASRSN:2187105.n: While at cruise at FL340, we experienced a R FWD Window EICAS message that resulted from an electrical arc and shattering of the right forward (R1) window. The QRH procedure was followed and the flight diverted to ZZZ with a [request for priority handling]. All company procedures were observed and the flight made a normal landing with no further abnormalities. We were flying at FL340 and experienced a R FWD Window EICAS message that resulted from an electrical arc of the right forward (R1) window. We followed the QRH procedure and diverted to ZZZ [requesting priority handling]. All company procedures were performed and the flight made a normal landing with no further abnormalities.
ASRSN:2187105.s: The flight crew at FL340 experienced an electrical arc and shattering of the right forward window, triggering an EICAS message. They followed QRH procedures, diverted to ZZZ with priority handling, and completed a normal landing with no further abnormalities.

ASRSN:2187126.n: Descended into icing. Pack 1 overheat caution first, then E1 anti-ice fail next, then wing anti- ice fail, finally a master warning that the anti-ice system is inop. We then climbed up out of the layer after declining an emergency, we ran the appropriate QRH procedures and was able to land in ZZZ.
ASRSN:2187126.s: The crew descended into icing, triggering pack overheat and anti-ice system failures. After climbing out of the layer and running QRH procedures, they declined an emergency and landed safely in ZZZ.

ASRSN:2187129.n: While on descent into ZZZ from ZZZ1, we were cleared to cross ZZZZZ at 13,000. At this point, we were at 19,000 and we had already gotten the ATIS and loaded, bugged, and briefed the ILS for Runway XXL. We started descending for ZZZZZ and as we were about to run the descent checklist, we noticed a 'flap low rate' awareness message appear. This message lasted for about 10 seconds. The Captain then deployed the speed brakes to begin slowing down, and about 5 seconds later, we had a 'flap fail' message appear on the EICAS. We identified and canceled and began running the QRH. We thoroughly went through the QRH and once we gathered and analyzed all available and pertinent information, we decided to [request priority handling] due to the fact our Vapp was close to max tire speed, and the weather conditions in ZZZ, which was reported wind around 300 @ 19 gusting 24 range as well as wet runways. As a result, we decided it would be best as well to change to Runway XXR for the added runway length. At this point, we established and communicated a plan, notified ATC we were [requesting priority handling] and requested the trucks to be rolled, notified the flight attendants, Dispatch, and passengers, and requested a long straight in final. As we were on the downwind, we ran the flap fail descent checklist and at around a 15 mile final we got configured and completed the flap fail landing checklist. We then continued to the runway, landed in the touchdown zone, and came to a stop on the runway. We got on the discrete frequency to talk to the trucks and advise them we would like them to check us out to make sure there was no issues, and after they thoroughly checked us out and advised us everything looked normal, we elected to taxi to the gate as the brake temps stayed in the green and there were no anomalies seen by rescue. The trucks followed us to the gate and we pulled into the gate without any further issues. Once we got to the gate, MX (Maintenance) was waiting for us and advised us the plane had been having flap issues. The Captain wrote the issue up, and the event ended there. During the descent into ZZZ from ZZZ1 we had built bugged briefed the approach to Runway XXL. We were reaching the top of descent at 19000 to cross ZZZZZ at 13000, about to complete the descent checklist, and as we started to pitch down, we noticed 'Flap low rate' pop up momentarily and went away as we noticed it. I then pulled out about 1/4 speed brake to begin slowing down. About 4 seconds later the EICAS message 'FLAP FAIL' came up. We identified and canceled then began running the QRH. We had made no adjustments to the flaps so we had nowhere to 'return to previous position' so continued with the QRH. In the process of deciding whether to [request priority handling] we began retrieving landing data and coefficient for Flaps failed indicating 0, at 68xxx lbs we used 70,000 lbs numbers to get a VAPP of 182 with slats 3, flaps 0 and 6564 factored landing distance (1.83). We decided to [request priority handling] because of our proximity to Max tire speed and current weather in ZZZ 300@19 (ish) combined with a wet runway. We decided to make the change to Runway XXR for the added runway length for extra safety in slowing down with the wet conditions and high approach speed. We returned to establish and communicate a plan, [requested priority handling] with ATC and gave all pertinent information and requested trucks to be rolled for us and inspection after landing and stopping on the runway. Messaged Dispatch and notified them of flap failure and [request of priority handling]. Called flight attendants and notified them of the [priority handling], flap failure and increased approach speed, I did not order a brace command, and told them we would be landing and stopping on the runway for inspection in case we got hot brakes from the faster approach speed. We returned to the QRH, requested a long straight in final. I discussed whether we should make an announcement with the FO, we decided to make one to brief them on the presence of the trucks and plan to stop on the runway after landing because of a technical issue with the plane and just using this as an added safety precaution. In the downwind I decided to extend the flaps to position 1 wait 10 seconds and return them to 0 in order to verify that they would extend slats which verified we were using the correct QRH and landing numbers as well as verify that the flaps were indeed failed because they had failed when we had made no adjustments to them. They operated as expected, flaps stayed at 0 but slats came to 3 which confirmed our numbers and plan. We finished the flap fail descent and then on a 12 mile final got configured and completed the Flap fail Landing checklist. We landed in the touchdown zone, rolled out and stopped on the runway. I pulled up the EICAS status page and checked our brake temps which were about 90ish and 120ish degrees Celsius a side, but still requested the fire trucks inspect the aircraft to make sure there wasn't anything going on we didn't have an indication of. There was not and we elected to taxi to our gate. Upon arriving to the gate, I wrote up the Flap fail and details of the event in the MX (Maintenance) report and called Dispatch then MX to inform them of the write up. Suggestions: The training we have received set us up wonderfully to be prepared and to handle this situation.
ASRSN:2187129.s: During descent into ZZZ, the flight crew encountered a 'flap fail' EICAS message after a brief 'flap low rate' alert. They executed the QRH, requested priority handling, and landed safely on Runway XXR with flaps zero and slats three, followed by a maintenance inspection.

ASRSN:2187136.n: After midfield crossing, while flying parallel to rwy XX on parallel heading, near miss with company Aircraft Y. Discussed with Flight Instructor (IP) flying Aircraft Y VFR bonanza in area was not on either practice area frequency or ZZZ within 5miles of ZZZ. Aircraft Y was on x/wind departure and bonanza interrupted his climb making Aircraft Y a primary hazard to my operation. I maintained visual separation from both, but due to terrain, and traffic proximity both above crossing from right to left I would have had few options to avoid. We were at 2000 feet in vicinity (VC) on terrain s of ZZZ at 100 knots. Turned for pattern entry early. Close proximity to other aircraft entering downwind, upon crosswind departure another aircraft was flying overhead, which caused us to halt climb, aircraft entering downwind called midfield crossing. After arresting climb, turn to the south west was made to avoid terrain in flight path, causing traffic conflict with aircraft entering downwind.
ASRSN:2187136.s: The pilot reported a near miss with a company aircraft and a VFR Bonanza while at 2,000 feet south of ZZZ during a crosswind departure. The Bonanza interrupted the company aircraft's climb, and terrain constraints forced an early turn that created a conflict with another aircraft entering the downwind leg.

ASRSN:2187303.n: As we started taxiing in ZZZZ I was the only one in the back galley getting my safety demonstration equipment and my FA #4 was getting into position for the safety demonstration overwing. I noticed the odor was like a plastic/rubber smell but it went away as the pilots started the engines. We performed the safety demonstration and when I came back I noticed the smell. As we sat down for takeoff my FA #4 asked if she could turn off the coffee pot warmers and I told her yes." At that point I figured the smell came from the coffee pot warmers as sometimes coffee spills on that metal hot plate. As we were getting ready for the service I noticed the smell but since we had turned on the warmers and started brewing the coffee didn't think too much of it. We did the service and noticed it as we got back to the galley. After we picked up the trash I sat down and ate. After like 5 minutes my FA #4 comes to me and asks if I can smell a rubbery/plastic smell. I told her I did and at that point it was stronger. She went up and told the FA #1 so at that point FA #1 came to the back to assess. She smelled it 3 to 4 rows from the back galley, it got stronger as she went into the back galley, and she saw a haze in the galley. At that point she informed the Captain and he advised us to turn everything off and wait 10 minutes to see if the odor subsided and to keep him informed.At that point I became used to the odor and could not smell it anymore but my FA #1 was still smelling it. The FA #3 came to the back and she noticed the odor 3 to 4 rows from the back galley as well. At this point the Captain decided we were going to make a rapid descent and do a [priority handling] landing into ZZZ with emergency vehicles meeting the aircraft as a precaution he did not want to take any chances in case there was something else going on that we could not see. We made the [priority handling] landing, ZZZ emergency vehicles assessed the aircraft using heat detection equipment, and they proceeded to follow us to the terminal. The odor did dissipate as we got on the ground. About 45 minutes before landing I started to get a headache rating a 6 from a scale of 1 to 10 (1 being mild and 10 being severe), very dry eyes, and exhausted/tired feeling. The Captain told us this was going to be written as a fume/odor event, Maintenance came and talked to each one of us, then a ZZZ Manager talked to us. He asked how we're feeling - 3 of us had headaches, red eyes, and exhaustion. He advised us we could go straight to our layover hotel or we can go to the hospital to get blood work done for carbon monoxide poisoning. When we decided we were going to the hospital to get tested whoever he was talking to on the other side was not happy with the response we gave him it almost seems like they were disregarding the entire fume event. We proceeded to the hospital via rideshare after being on the phone for 30 minutes just to file a report and start the process.Fume events NEED to be handled differently and faster. This whole calling to file a report to talk to a nurse to assess AND then we choose whether or not we want to go to the hospital based on nurse recommendations should NOT be handled like this! So much time wasted ESPECIALLY when we have a 4-hour window to get blood drawn! There needs to be a faster way to get this done. Furthermore the attitudes from managers is NOT appreciated especially when we tell them what our symptoms are! In addition, having to call out sick, then file a report, and then get it recategorized should not be the case, it almost seems like we are getting penalized for even reporting a fume event. The fact that if we had worse symptoms, having to worry if we would be pay protected for the trip since we were working and having to a get "sick" before we file to get it recategorized SHOULD NOT have to be this way at all, the airlines' priority should be for us not to worry about that and make a seamless process. Fix this process and make it BLACKAND WHITE!"
ASRSN:2187303.s: Cabin crew reported a rubbery odor and haze in the rear galley during taxi and takeoff at ZZZZ, causing headaches and dry eyes. The Captain executed a priority landing at ZZZ with emergency response, where ground crews found no heat source, though the crew criticized the delayed medical assessment process for potential fume exposure.

ASRSN:2187370.n: I filed an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to ZZZ1. As part of the preflight I checked the pitot heat was operational as I knew I would be climbing through a thin layer to 4000 feet and it was hot. About an hour and fifteen minutes into the flight we entered some light IMC and noticed my airspeed indicator was jumping around at about 0 degrees Celsius. I requested lower to get to warmer temperatures and as I descended the temperature didn't change and the airspeed kept lowering to 60 knots and then to 0 knots indicated airspeed although the manifold pressure and rpm were correct for the descent. The groundspeed on the GPS was also correct. The altitude indicator was erratic. The attitude indicator on the Aspen E1000 suddenly turned 90 degrees to the left however, the backup gyro/vacuum driven attitude indicator did not. I was without airspeed and altitude indications in IMC. I radioed to [request priority handling] but I don't know if that was ever heard as after several attempts, I did not receive a response. I switched to the alternate static source and continued a slow descent until I broke through the layer at about 1500 feet. I was then contacted by an aircraft relaying a message from ATC. I reported to them that I was circling to land at ZZZ2. Upon changing frequencies and locating the airport I radioed on XXX.XX that I was entering downwind, base and final. Upon landing the runway had about 4 inches of slush and a quartering, gusting headwind that continued to push the aircraft sideways. Without any traction and with full rudder and aileron I was unable to keep the aircraft on the runway, striking a runway light before regaining control and taxiing to the FBO. Once in the hangar, I tested the pitot heat again. There was no voltage drop and no heat on the pitot tube. I believe the pitot heat failed during flight causing it to ice up and also causing the failure of other flight instruments.
ASRSN:2187370.s: A pilot flying an IFR flight encountered pitot heat failure in IMC, causing erroneous airspeed and altitude indications and an Aspen E1000 attitude indicator malfunction. After descending to 1500 feet and landing on a slushy runway, the pilot lost directional control and struck a runway light before taxiing to the FBO.

ASRSN:2187387.n: While practicing the ZZZ Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP) out of ZZZ from runway XXR, we had just taken our initial left turn to intercept the ZZZ [VOR] radial outbound, at 2800 msl and about 1300 AGL we had a large loss of engine power. At the time the student, a CFI training for CFII, was flying and I, instructor immediately took controls. I turned us into the left downwind for XXL the north runway. The initial power loss lasted about 5 seconds of the engine sputtering and rough running. The best way I can explain it is like the normal shutdown procedure when you bring the mixture to idle cut off. Again, after the first indication of an issue we had a positive 3 way change of flight controls as I turned downwind for the north runway. I communicated to the tower I was having an engine issue and making left traffic and would advise momentarily what I needed. By this point I had verified that the throttle and mixture were full forward, carb heat was off, fuel pump and mags all on, and that the fuel selector was fully seated in the right detent. The engine instruments were all in the green with the oil pressure around 60 psi, engine was making around 2000 rpm at this point. The engine seemed to come back to full power for about 5 seconds as I kept it at VY 76 to get as much altitude as possible. But after that we had another shutter and drop in rpms just prior to entering the normal downwind. The RPM was fluctuating rapidly, and it was like we would get steady rpms for 2 seconds then it would drop, come back, but then have a little less than the previous cycle. By this time, I had [requested priority handling] and the tower controller did a great job coordinating the 6 or so aircraft out of our way. Again, I had taken off XXR from the south side, and they offered me either XXL or XYR on the north side. With the throttle full and the power partial, at 76kts we only were losing about 100 fpm. With where I was in the pattern I felt comfortable making back around to runway XXL. By this point I had the CFI I was flying with reference the checklist and verify everything was correct. The only thing we did not do was swap fuel tanks. We had partial power loss and for the most part was able to maintain minimal altitude loss, so I felt swapping tanks came with the risk of making it worse. As I passed abeam the thousand foot markers, we were about 1000 agl so in the normal position for the power off 180 approaches we practice. By this time ATC had moved everyone off final and above us so I started the power off approach. I told the student I was with that I was starting the turn and if he thought I was getting high, low, fast, slow, or if anything started looking wrong, to communicate it to me. As we started the descent the engine got very quiet. We successfully and safely made the approach and touched down on the 1000 footers. The throttle was brought back and oddly enough the engine idled at 1000 rpms without issue. As I gave some throttle to get off the active, any setting over 1200 rpms resulted in rough running. We were able to limp it off of taxiway and onto the north ramp. We shut down and called our dispatch for a tow. The entire event was about 4-5 minutes from takeoff to touch down. Prior to take off we preformed the runup without issue, then held short for about 20 minutes waiting for takeoff. During that hold short time we did not swap tanks or do anything outside of the normal, before takeoff check list. On take off the engine instruments were all in the green like normal.
ASRSN:2187387.s: An instructor and student experienced intermittent engine power loss during an obstacle departure procedure from runway XXR. The instructor executed a priority landing on runway XXL after verifying controls and fuel settings, attributing the issue to rough running that persisted above 1200 RPM.

ASRSN:2187405.n: Another instrument-rated pilot and I were aiming to regain proficiency as it had been sometime since either of us had practiced approaches. After he had flown as PIC from ZZZ1 to ZZZ, it was my turn and I planned, briefed, and filed an IFR plan to ZZZ2 from there, expecting MVFR conditions.After pre-flight and before startup, I called clearance delivery for my clearance, which consisted of fly ODP (Obstacle Departure Procedure) then radar vectors to ZZZ2, climb to 5000, and contact ZZZ approach on frequency. At this point, I briefed the ODP, set my heading bug to 150 and ZZZ VOR for the radial. After run-up was complete and I was holding short of RWY XX at ZZZ, I then called clearance delivery again for my release, at which point they advised me the departure frequency had changed to another frequency and I was cleared for departure and void if not off in 5 minutes (departure window: local time XA:37 to XA:42).I reset the standby frequency to ZZZ approach and updated my CRAFT clearance notes to reflect the change. With no other traffic in the pattern, I self-announced and took runway XX and turned left to heading 150 (I should have turned right per the ODP). After climbing thru 1200, I made my last call to the CTAF and hailed ZZZ departure on frequency, when they immediately advised me I had a low altitude alert. After I stated I was performing the ODP, they advised I was performing it incorrectly. At this point, they advised an immediate climb to 6000 ft and an emergency vector to 360. After I was above 3000 ft, I was given a phone number to copy for a possible deviation.Contributing factors: Re-briefing procedure after adjusting plans and updating notes: The combination of a last minute change and short (to a newer pilot) void-if-not-off-by time put me in a 'hurried' state, and I should have asked for more time to get setup and re-brief before departing. Text-based ODP: I believe a visualization of the ODP on documents would have helped prevent my mistake. I looked at my IFR Low chart to visualize what I was going to do, and without the hills to the west on the VFR charts, there was nothing immediately obvious to me that turning to the south would be dangerous. Upon taking off and turning, I also saw the hills, but in a lightly loaded high performance aircraft good climb performance it wasn't obvious that terrain would be a factor (I'd also flown ZZZ RWY XX left crosswind departure when flying VFR previously multiple times).
ASRSN:2187405.s: The pilot departed ZZZ RWY XX intending to fly an ODP but turned left instead of right due to a hurried re-brief after a last-minute frequency change. This incorrect turn triggered a low altitude alert, forcing ATC to issue an emergency climb to 6000 ft and vector to heading 360.

ASRSN:2187409.n: I was flying north, returning to ZZZ. A large group of airplanes were to my northeast with a flight path to the north west, so our paths were converging. This particular incident was not a big deal, I have in-cockpit ADSB traffic, so I had plenty of time to descend prior to meeting the intersecting traffic (I passed well below). But because Big Sky Approach has no coherent frequency plans, I didn't think about tuning up Big Sky Approach and seeing if they were talking to the aircraft that I was converging with. For all I knew, they might've been putting them on a descent and my descent would've further complicated the situation. That didn't happen, but it could have. We've got a situation where Big Sky Approach flips frequency sectors around based on active runway at BOI. When I fly near controlled airports, I routinely monitor the appropriate frequency. Why? If I'm causing a problem, I want to know so I can do something different. The SLC sectional instructs 126.9 if north of BOI, and 119.6 if south. Meanwhile, BOI airport data says use 126.9 frequency if within 15 NM, and 119.6 if greater. Neither the chart nor the airport data resembles how Approach assigns area frequencies. You can't look at official information and determine what Big Sky is doing. In meetings available to local pilots, Big Sky Controllers explain how they actually manage frequency sectors, and it has nothing to do with the published information. Rather 126.9 is used for handling finals and 119.6 most everywhere else. This has gone on for years. I get that Boise Approach needs to manage the best way they know how. However, I take objection to a frequency plan that can't be communicated via the chart or an airport data. Either update the information on the chart and in the airport data to reflect how you actually manage the frequency sectors, or come up with a frequency plan that's capable of being communicated through official channels. To their credit, Controllers are usually friendly and professional about getting VFR traffic on the frequency they want you on, but that only fixes the issue for those who a) want to talk to Approach, and b) Approach has to have available bandwidth to set up flight following. This is sloppy management. Please fix it so the information is congruent with practice.
ASRSN:2187409.s: A pilot flying VFR north toward ZZZ noted a potential conflict with converging traffic but descended safely using ADS-B. The pilot attributed the risk to Big Sky Approach's uncoordinated frequency plan, which contradicts published charts and airport data, creating confusion about which frequency to monitor.

ASRSN:2187431.n: On departure from ZZZ on the ZZZZZ departure SID. Upon reaching 700' after taking off on Runway XXR, auto pilot and nav function of auto pilot was activated. The airplane rolled to the right, and before we could correct, Departure control directed us to turn immediately to 110 degrees. After we were steady on that heading, we were asked to contact ZZZ ATC after we were safely on the ground. On departure from ZZZ on the ZZZZZ SID, upon reaching 700' Auto Pilot and NAV was activated. The airplane rolled right and before we could correct, Departure Control directed us to an immediate turn to head 110.
ASRSN:2187431.s: Pilots reported that after activating autopilot and NAV at 700 feet on the ZZZZZ SID from Runway XXR, the aircraft rolled right. Departure Control immediately directed a turn to heading 110, and the crew was instructed to contact ZZZ ATC after landing.

ASRSN:2187465.n: While taxiing into the gate at ZZZ, it was observed that a super tug from the ground crew was positioned within the Operational Safety Zone (OSZ). After communication was made station operations, the super tug was moved back to appear outside of the OSZ.The aircraft continued taxiing toward the gate. At approximately 20 feet from the stop line, the super tug unexpectedly pulled forward back into the OSZ. This sudden action created a significant hazard, requiring the aircraft to come to an immediate stop to avoid a potential collision. Once the aircraft was stopped, the tug driver quickly reversed back to a position outside the OSZ.The reason for the tug driver's decision to re- enter the OSZ at such close proximity to the aircraft is unclear. This action posed a serious safety risk and was deemed an egregious deviation from standard operational procedures.
ASRSN:2187465.s: During taxiing at ZZZ, a ground crew super tug unexpectedly re-entered the Operational Safety Zone 20 feet from the stop line, forcing the aircraft to stop immediately to avoid collision. The driver's reason for this hazardous maneuver is unclear, though it was deemed an egregious deviation from standard procedures.

ASRSN:2187485.n: We were in cruise at FL370 in smooth air when we encountered a Mountain Wave event. We were southwest of ZZZ. The onset of the wave was very smooth and fast. There was no turbulence associated with the wave. The wave caused an increase in airspeed and altitude. We estimated the wave was plus 25 knots and caused a ballooning, (increase) in altitude of approximately 360 feet. We also experienced a very slight overspeed of approximately 2 knots into the barber pole for four seconds. We were in the process of notifying ATC when they called us at the same time and noticed the event as it was happening. The pilot flying disconnected the autopilot system and recovered the aircraft to the correct altitude and airspeed then re-engaged the autopilot once the wave passed. After notifying ATC we notified dispatch and entered an Electronic Log Book (ELB) entry to maintenance about the event. After landing I called the Chief Pilot and verbally debriefed the event. Level cruise flight , we encountered a rogue mountain wave that was immediate without any buffet or warning .. auto pilot was engaged / auto throttles engaged but auto flight couldn't control the updraft. We suspected the airspeed was at .81-.82 for maybe 5 seconds after the encounter This rogue mountain wave was instantaneous with really no time to prepare for this event - no other aircraft reported any mountain wave activity prior to us getting into it. No aircraft damage was suspected - and we continued on to our destination
ASRSN:2187485.s: During cruise at FL370 southwest of ZZZ, the crew encountered an unforecast mountain wave that caused a 360-foot altitude gain and a brief 2-knot overspeed. The pilot flying manually disconnected the autopilot to recover the aircraft, and no damage was reported.

ASRSN:2187494.n: While on the Tipp Toe Visual 28L approach to SFO, NorCal Approach issued a descend and maintain 3000 clearance between EDDYY and SIDBY. The PF engaged LVL CHG after I set 3000 in the ALT SET window and the aircraft began a descent. We were subsequently cleared for the approach and told to maintain 180 knots until the San Mateo bridge. PF then asked to set TDZE. I set 100 in the ALT SET window. We finished configuring the aircraft for landing and completed the Landing Checklist. PF attempted to close the speed window by pressing the speed intervene button, when it didn't close, I tried to press it. I realized at that point that the selected mode was still LVL CHG. I pressed VNAV twice but it did not engage. The PF disengaged the autopilot and leveled the aircraft. At the same moment ATC issued an altitude alert with our call sign. The FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) mode was in LVL change until about 950' AGL and we descended below glide path at approximately 3 mile final. Glide path was recaptured, the approach was stable at 500' and the landing was uneventful.
ASRSN:2187494.s: During a visual approach to SFO, the crew descended below the glide path because the autopilot remained in LVL CHG mode after a failed VNAV engagement attempt. The pilot disengaged the autopilot to level the aircraft following an ATC altitude alert, but the approach was stabilized and the landing was uneventful.

ASRSN:2187514.n: Sorry if this is too wordy. First report submission and not necessarily a specific chain of events that led directly to the lower glideslope.I haven't flown into Austin many times and it had been awhile since my last flight there. Ultimately we received a momentary low visual glideslope indication (4 red on the PAPI) and a single glideslope auditory call out at approximately 300 ft AGL but the thrust and pitch corrections were already made (minor vertical adjustments at this distance) and the external environmental factors allowed for us to continue the approach to an uneventful landing.We received vectors from Approach Control off of the WLEEE7 approach. We were given multiple speed assignments slowing us down with the final instruction to slow to 170. We needed flaps 5 to slow to 170. We were previously configured flaps 1 with speed brakes to slow us to 190 (if I recall correctly). I put the speed brakes in and called for flaps 5 to slow to 170. Around this same time we were told we had a 40 not overtake on previous traffic. No issues with altitudes on the arrival.Once we were slowed to 170, the controller started to vector us to the visual which kept us about 4 miles behind the previous landing traffic and left us on a base vs a dogleg which drove me to use the digital display of the final course more so than the external visuals. The ATIS called for gusty winds that required a 15kt. additive for our target speed (I believe it was 220 11 gust 21).
